items.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005
items.q: He came the contractor. He says, “Kid, I’m going to get you here.” And I started at the Orpheum Theater. Then after a while he got the job at The Frolicks night club, only a couple of blocks, where Louis Prima was. He was playing in another place.

ctx.x: That’s interesting so maybe like ninth grade or so? You got to ninth or tenth grade?

Right. Well at that time it was eighth grade and then started first year. Yeah. But Howard Vorhees got me the job at the Forest Club. It was a gambling house. They didn’t call them casinos then. And we would play for dancing and so forth while people gambled. And then he finally got me to go into the Orpheum Theater. He came the contractor. He says, “Kid, I’m going to get you here.” And I started at the Orpheum Theater. Then after a while he got the job at The Frolicks night club, only a couple of blocks, where…
At that time, in New Orleans, King Oliver and Louis Armstrong, those guys had already gone north.

items.title: Spiegle Willcox and Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Norwich, New York, November 14, 1995
items.q: A block or two down was another youngster, Louis Prima. Because he was from New Orleans also.

ctx.x: I was born in Chicago, June 20, 1913. And in 1927, the spring of ‘27, George Evans, who is still alive and lives in Pensacola, he asked my mother and father if he could take me on the road. I wasn’t even fourteen. I never forgot this. And we had trumpet, two saxes, drums, bass and a singer. No trombone. And we were playing, oh, Dixieland tunes, whatever was popular at that time. Then after being in Florida, we went to Jacksonville © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

and Gainesville and Pensacola, I ended up in New Orleans. That was October of 1927. Now in those days, it was prohibition. I played in a night club called The Frolicks. The Frolicks. Where people drank the whiskey in coffee cups. A block or two down was another youngster, Louis Prima. Because he was from New Orleans also. And in those days, there were so many night clubs. You could leave one club tonight and go to another one. You must have had two dozen clubs in New Orleans. You can imagine what they had in…
